title: COP31 draft drops fossil-fuel phaseout language as climate talks near their deadline
subtitle: The revised negotiating text keeps proposals on electrification and adaptation finance but removes explicit calls to move away from fossil fuels. It is still a draft, with consequences that reach well beyond the summit hall.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: A revised draft of the COP31 climate summit’s overarching decision has removed explicit language calling for a transition away from fossil fuels and an accelerated phaseout, sharpening the question of what governments are prepared to promise in Antalya, Türkiye.

The UN climate secretariat published the nine-page version on 19 November, as talks approached their scheduled 20 November conclusion. It is a negotiating proposal, not an adopted agreement. Its wording can still change before governments approve a final outcome.

The difference is visible in the documents themselves. The 16 November draft explicitly urged implementation of the earlier global stocktake’s fossil-fuel transition language and called for accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels. The 19 November version contains no mention of “fossil”.
What the deletion does—and does not—mean

Removing an explicit commitment from a new proposal does not itself cancel an earlier decision. The revised text still calls for national climate and adaptation plans to be implemented with reference to the first global stocktake, the COP28 outcome adopted in 2023.

That distinction matters. Governments can point to the continuing reference to the stocktake, while critics can reasonably ask why the new cover decision no longer names the energy sources at the centre of the dispute. The political signal becomes less direct even where earlier commitments remain part of the negotiating framework.

Reuters reported that the summit’s Turkish and Australian leadership defended an emphasis on implementation and the difficulty of securing consensus. At a 19 November press conference, UN climate chief Simon Stiell said the process belonged to almost 200 parties and described achieving strong, balanced outcomes across the negotiations as complex but essential.

The disagreement is therefore about both substance and the route to agreement: whether a text acceptable to more governments can deliver faster action, or whether removing explicit language makes it harder to hold those governments to account.
Electricity is only part of the transition

The revised proposal retains a goal of increasing electricity’s share of total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035. It links that ambition with renewable capacity, energy efficiency, storage and stronger grids.

Electricity’s share of energy consumption is not the same measure as the share generated from clean sources. An electrification target needs to be assessed alongside how that electricity is produced, who can afford it and whether transmission networks can deliver it reliably.

For a household, a national investment plan becomes meaningful through a usable connection, dependable service and a bill it can pay. For workers and small businesses, the transition also concerns the skills and infrastructure needed to participate in changing energy markets. These are practical tests of implementation, not outcomes guaranteed by a summit percentage.

Carbon Brief’s account of the negotiations explains that the cover decision is only one part of a much wider set of texts. Separate negotiations also concern adaptation, finance and a just-transition mechanism. Judging the summit requires reading those outcomes together, rather than treating one paragraph as the whole settlement.
Who pays for protection?

Finance wording has changed too. The earlier draft proposed that tripling adaptation finance should reach at least US$120 billion. The revised version retains the call for efforts to triple adaptation finance by 2035, but asks for further work on the baseline and an implementation pathway.

The difference between a multiplier and an agreed starting point is consequential. Without knowing the baseline, readers cannot calculate what “triple” would deliver. Without a delivery pathway, they cannot tell when support should arrive or which institution is responsible for providing it.

Adaptation concerns protection from climate impacts, rather than only reducing the emissions that drive them. In practical terms, that can mean safer water systems, stronger health services and preparations for dangerous weather. Families need those protections to function where they live, including when household income is too limited to purchase alternatives.

The final test in Antalya is not simply whether negotiators finish a document. It is whether the outcome identifies responsibilities clearly enough for communities to assess delivery: emissions reductions, accessible finance and protections that reach people before the next emergency.

For women managing household budgets, children growing up with climate risks and communities seeking investment, ambiguous promises carry real costs. ATHENA will judge the agreement by what it makes possible—and by what governments can be held responsible for doing.
The Athena Perspective.
